text: Pause before you click. Urgency is the scammer’s favourite tool.
Install updates. They fix the security holes attackers use.
Back up your important files in two places, and test that you can restore them.
If you wouldn’t tell a stranger, don’t post it publicly.
Use a long passphrase of unrelated words instead of a short complicated password.
Never reuse a password. One leak should not open all your accounts.
Turn on two-factor authentication for email, banking and social media.
Never share a one-time code (OTP) with anyone, even if they say they are from your bank.
Don’t trust links in messages. Open the official app or type the address yourself.
Check the sender’s full address. Look-alike domains are common.
A message that mixes fear, a deadline and a link is a classic scam pattern.
Real banks never ask for your PIN, OTP or password by SMS, call or chat.
Use a strong screen lock and turn on find-my-device.
Install apps only from your official app store, not from links sent in chats.
If your phone suddenly loses all signal, call your network provider. It could be a SIM swap.
Deny app permissions that don’t match what the app does.
Turn on two-step verification on WhatsApp and never share its 6-digit code.
Don’t post photos of IDs, boarding passes or tickets.
If a friend suddenly asks for money, call them first. Their account may be hijacked.
Review who can see your posts, photos and phone number every few months.
Use your bank’s official app or the number on your card. Never numbers from a message.
Check the beneficiary name before confirming a transfer.
Shield your PIN at ATMs and POS terminals, and don’t accept help from strangers.
Set transaction alerts so you notice unusual debits quickly.
Share only the personal data that is really needed.
Write the purpose and date across photocopies of your ID.
Shred papers with account numbers and personal details.
Don’t paste passwords or private data into AI chat tools.
Check the web address before you type a password. The real site is before the first single slash.
Pop-ups that scare you (“your phone is infected”) are almost always scams. Close them.
Avoid cracked or pirated software. It often comes with malware.
On public Wi-Fi, avoid banking. Use mobile data instead.
If it promises guaranteed high returns with no risk, it’s a scam.
Never pay a fee to receive a prize, job, loan or scholarship.
Verify urgent money requests with a call to a number you already know.
Talk to someone you trust before you send money. Scammers hate a second opinion.
